summary: Planet X is a free web app that searches NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey for a distant, undiscovered planet. In a single image, a far-off planet looks just like a star, but it can't hide its parallax: SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months from opposite sides of Earth's orbit, so a planet 500 AU away appears to jump about 825″ between passes. For any patch of sky, the app pairs every SPHEREx image at the same wavelength, flags anything that moved, appeared or vanished, and weeds out cosmic rays, bad pixels, and known asteroids and stars, leaving a short list of candidates for people to check. On real data it found asteroid 16 Psyche within 1.3″ of JPL's prediction, and in tests on six real fields it caught 80–91% of bright planted movers without inventing any. It also measures the SPHEREx spectra of stars, estimates distance from parallax and takes in new data releases without code changes. Anyone with a browser can join the hunt for distant worlds, and the app is honest about its limits: a typical Planet Nine is too faint for a single SPHEREx image.
details:
We wanted to find a planet that's too far away and too faint to stand out in a single picture. In any one image, a distant planet looks exactly like a star. But it can't hide its parallax. SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, and because Earth is on the opposite side of the Sun each time, a planet 500 AU away seems to jump about 825″ between passes. Its real movement in that time is only about 58″.

So we built a web app that hunts for that jump. It pulls every SPHEREx exposure of a patch of sky from NASA's archive and lines up passes taken at the same wavelength. That part was trickier than we expected, since SPHEREx sees in 102 colors. Then it looks for anything that appeared, disappeared or moved. Most of those turn out to be cosmic rays, bad pixels or known asteroids, so the app checks each one against the SPHEREx pipeline's flags, JPL's asteroid catalog and Gaia's star catalog. What's left goes on a short list for a person to look at. You can explore the whole sky, blink between scans, play them like a video, and click on anything suspicious to inspect it. Click any star and the app measures its SPHEREx spectrum on the fly, from 0.75 to 5 µm, using every exposure that covers it; the brown dwarf pair Epsilon Indi B shows its methane dip. Without the server, the hosted version shows spectra saved for the example targets and the brightest stars around them.

It also follows the challenge's suggestions: you can subtract and stack passes, overlay Gaia stars, see other telescopes' images of the same patch, check the pipeline's contamination flags, and share a link with the coordinates in the URL. The five test targets from the challenge are one-click examples.

Benefits

It turns a huge pile of survey images into a list someone can actually go through. We tested it on real data, and it found the asteroid 16 Psyche within 1.3″ of where JPL said it would be. We also planted fake moving objects into six real SPHEREx fields to see how well it catches them. It found 80–91% of the bright ones and never reported a mover that wasn't there. We also built a tool that predicts where a vanished object should reappear, and another that estimates how far away it is from how much it shifted. And when SPHEREx releases new data, you can add it without touching the code.

Intended impact

We'd like anyone, whether a student, an amateur astronomer or a researcher, to be able to search for distant Solar System objects using free NASA data and a browser. We were also honest with ourselves about the limits. A single SPHEREx image isn't deep enough to see a typical Planet Nine, and we think knowing exactly where those limits are is useful for whoever searches next.

Tools we used

JavaScript for the app and the detection code, three.js for the 3D sky, Aladin Lite for other telescopes' views of the same patch, and a small Node.js server, plus a Python/FastAPI version, to fetch real data. The data comes from NASA's IRSA archive (SPHEREx), NASA's Deep Star Maps, JPL's small-body tools, ESA's Gaia DR3, and sky surveys and SIMBAD names from the Strasbourg Astronomical Data Center (CDS). We hosted it on GitHub Pages and used Playwright to test it in a real browser. The code, tests and documentation were written with an AI coding assistant, Claude by Anthropic, working from our direction; we reviewed, ran and verified everything. The in-app helper uses Google's Gemini, through Firebase AI Logic, only for questions its hand-written notes don't cover, with those notes as its only source, and labels those replies "AI answer". No special hardware is needed; it runs in any browser.

What's creative about it

Most searches try to spot something faint. We look for the one thing a distant planet can't hide: its motion against the background as Earth moves around the Sun. SPHEREx's six-month rhythm gives us that baseline for free. We also put a sky viewer, a real detection pipeline and a review workflow into one page, and the app always tells you whether you're looking at live, saved or simulated data.

What we thought about

  • Comparing images at the same wavelength, so color changes don't look like motion
  • Weeding out everything that isn't a planet: asteroids, variable stars, brown dwarfs, cosmic rays and bad pixels
  • Never claiming a discovery; everything is a candidate for a human to check
  • Making it easy to use, with Simple and Advanced modes, a phone layout, and a hosted version that works without a server
  • Keeping it useful as more SPHEREx data comes out
